title: Collective Life in Marysin: Youth and Children Organize in the Łódź Ghetto
summary: The Marysin collectives offer a revealing account of young people trying to sustain shared work and community life inside the ghetto.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Organization of the former students collective

editorialContent:
## A community made under confinement

Marysin’s collectives began in a place transformed by persecution. German authorities forced Łódź’s Jews into a ghetto established in early 1940; the ghetto was sealed on April 30. Within that enclosure, Marysin stood out as a relatively green, semi-rural district. It offered something scarce in the crowded city: patches of land where young people could work together, and space for communal life. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the ghetto’s wider reality—forced labor, severe overcrowding and hunger—while Yad Vashem’s account of Łódź specifically identifies the youth collectives in Marysin as agricultural communities. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/give-me-your-children-voices-from-the-lodz-ghetto?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book dates the establishment of collective farms and youth collectives to early May 1940, just after the ghetto’s closure. Its Hebrew wording describes “collective farms” being established; another passage names the Zionist party collectives in Marishin. Read together, these accounts preserve both the practical form of the project and its political diversity. The book names Gordonia, Hashomer Hatzair and Mizrachi among the participating movements. It does not give a full list of the collectives or explain their daily routines in detail, so those particulars should not be assumed from the brief testimony. The event appears in the book as [Collective groups established in Marysin](/communities/lodz/records/event_candidate_d7e7716c7d96d1ef47faba73) and [Collective groups in Marysin](/communities/lodz/records/mention_00ff8d715a83d195355b900c).

## Political movements, shared ground

The collectives were not politically uniform. Gordonia and Hashomer Hatzair belonged to the Zionist youth world, though they represented distinct currents; Mizrachi brought a religious-Zionist presence. The memorial book’s account thus points to separate organizations finding a shared foothold in Marysin, rather than a single movement directing all the young people there. Outside evidence supports the scale of the broader phenomenon: Yad Vashem reports that by the end of summer 1940 about 1,000 members of youth movements lived in Marysin, organized in 25 Zionist groups. Its Encyclopedia of the Ghettos says that during the ghetto’s first six months more than 1,000 movement members lived in communes, cultivated land and organized cultural activities. These are wider counts, not numbers supplied by the memorial-book passages about the particular groups it names. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/en/exhibitions/ready2print/pdf/there-is-a-land.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Marysin’s agricultural setting mattered, but the activity there was not simply farming. Yad Vashem describes communal training farms modeled on prewar frameworks, with each youth movement receiving a house and land. The aim, as Yad Vashem presents it, was to give young people purposeful activity and some distance from the distress and enforced idleness of ghetto life. The memorial book’s spare account does not itself spell out that motivation; it becomes clearer when placed alongside the independent historical record. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/en/exhibitions/ready2print/pdf/there-is-a-land.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Medem School’s former students

A different strand of collective life came from former students of the Medem School. The memorial book records that forty youths and children organized themselves in Marishin as a collective. It links this group to the Bund, which had founded the school. The school’s Yiddish-secular educational tradition therefore had a life beyond the classroom: former pupils carried a sense of organized community into the ghetto. The book’s account is brief, however; it does not provide the children’s names, ages, individual family histories, or the collective’s precise daily arrangements. The event is recorded as [Organization of the former students collective](/communities/lodz/records/event_candidate_3bf96ae0adec12a72791c48e), and the institution as [Medem School](/communities/lodz/records/mention_732b0feb2c5d08fabd725050). The linked [Former Students Collective](/communities/lodz/records/mention_769e92a8a96b2c7d5ab6f066) is described as funded by the [Bund](/communities/lodz/records/mention_a0d9f2d3fa61971b92eae564) and affiliated with [Rumkowski](/communities/lodz/records/mention_6a803064ae6dedcfcd546b0d); the supplied evidence does not explain the exact terms of that funding or affiliation.

The group of forty should not be confused with the larger Marysin movement collectives. The memorial book presents it as a distinct initiative by former Medem pupils; Yad Vashem’s aggregate estimate of roughly 1,000 youth-movement members describes the broader district and its various groups. These figures answer different questions, and the sources do not establish whether the forty were included in a particular count. Nor does the book’s account of the former pupils establish that this specific group farmed land or followed the same program as the Zionist training collectives.

The Bund’s presence also belonged to a wider political landscape. The community record describes competition between the Bund and Communists in Łódź’s workers’ quarter; it also names youth frameworks such as Tsukunft and Zukunft. That context helps explain why a Bund-founded school and its former pupils mattered: collective organization was not only a response to material hardship, but also a continuation of political and educational commitments. Still, the evidence provided does not identify the forty children individually or show how their collective related to other Bund youth groups.

## Children, culture and the shrinking space for community

Independent sources add evidence of children’s institutions and cultural activity in Marysin beyond the two kinds of collectives described in the memorial-book records. Yad Vashem’s account of survivor Franka Kleczewska says that children’s homes, schools and pioneer training groups operated there. Its account of ghetto culture also notes that youth-organization clubs in Marysin held performances until the end of 1942. This wider record suggests a district where agricultural work, education, care and cultural activity overlapped—but it does not prove that the former Medem students’ collective ran any particular school, home or performance. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/en/exhibitions/albums/franka-kleczewska.asp?utm_source=openai))

The initiatives were fragile. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos reports that the Marysin farms were dissolved in January 1941 and that young people returned to the ghetto, where some continued political and social activity secretly. Its account of cultural performances places an endpoint later, at the end of 1942. These dates need not contradict each other: agricultural communes could be dismantled while youth groups and clubs persisted in altered forms. The sources describe different aspects of collective life, not necessarily one institution continuing unchanged. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/YV/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=516&utm_source=openai))

The memorial book preserves what a bare institutional chronology cannot: the fact that young people organized, and that former pupils made a community for children in the middle of forced confinement. Its testimony is limited and leaves many names and relationships unknown. The wider archival record establishes that Marysin’s collectives were part of a larger network of youth activity, but cannot fill in the identities of the forty former Medem students from the evidence available here. Their organization remains both a historical fact and an unfinished question for further research.
